paragraphs: Describe the chemical nature of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and their enzymes.
Explain enzyme action and factors influencing their action.
What is our food actually made up of?
The majority of compounds we obtain from food fall into three categories:
Each of these substances plays an important role in our body; furthermore, each substance is broken down by our body in different ways.
What are carbohydrates, and why do we need them?
Carbohydrates are a diverse group of molecules that are composed of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms.
These elements are often  arranged in a 1:2:1 ratio                     (roughly 1C : 2H : 1O)... glucose, for example, is a carbohydrate with the chemical formula C6H12O6
The main role of carbohydrates is to provide energy for the               body; we are unable to synthesize them ourselves (unlike plants!), so we must obtain them from other sources (food)
Carbohydrates are found in all plant-based foods (e.g. fruits, vegetables, and grains).
Single sugar unit which contains between 3-8 carbons
Can switch between chain and cyclic forms
Carbohydrates with the same chemical formula but arranged in different ways are referred to as isomers
The three monosaccharides shown on the left are isomers because they all contain 6 C, 12 H, and 6 O
Also a type of reducing sugar
Formed by the “linking together” of monosaccharides.

This is accomplished by a process known as dehydration synthesis, or condensation, which involves the loss of a hydroxide (OH-) ion from one monomer and hydrogen ion from another in order to form a bond between the single sugar units.
Dehydration synthesis thus leads to the release of water (H2O) as a by-product.
Contain two sugar units and more than 7 carbon atoms

Common examples of disaccharides include sucrose (formed by the reaction between glucose and fructose), maltose (formed by the reaction between two glucose molecules), and lactose (formed by the reaction between glucose and galactose)
“Complex carbohydrates” with many simple sugars linked together.
Cellulose is more difficult for our bodies to break down than simple sugars; offer little energy as a result, but are a good source of fibre.
What are lipids, and why do we need them?

Like carbohydrates, lipids are also composed of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms. However, in lipids, these atoms are arranged into molecules called “fatty acids” (a hydrocarbon chain bonded to a carboxyl group). Fatty acids are the building blocks of lipids. Three fatty acids are typically attached to a glycerol backbone making a complete lipid.
The carboxyl group (-COOH) is what distinguishes lipids from carbohydrates. This group causes lipids to be non-polar, which is why they tend to repel water and have a waxy or oily consistency.
Lipids have a number of important roles in our bodies. They act to store energy, are a component of our cell membranes, help carry vitamins, and play a role in hormone synthesis.
Lipids are found in foods which contain animal-based fats and plant-based oils.
Carbon chain consists only of single bonds, leading to a more “rectangular”shape, which allows chains to pack together easily
Tend to be solids at room temperature and are more difficult to break down (i.e. butter); typically from animals
At least one double bond in the carbon chain leads to a “kinked”shape, meaning that chains cannot easily be packed together
Tend to be liquids at room temperature and are easier to break down (i.e. olive oil); typically from plants
Hydrogenation is used to convert unsaturated fats (i.e. oils) into saturated fats (i.e. butter). This involves the breaking of double bonds and addition of hydrogen…

Converting “good” fats (unsaturated) into “bad” fats (saturated) seems counterintuitive, but it allows us to create products in solid form rather than liquid form; often preferable for cooking/baking.
Formed by the union of glycerol molecule (a 3-carbon lipid) and three fatty acids through the process of dehydration synthesis
Triglycerides that are solid at room temperature are called fats (tend to be saturated, and are derived from animals)
Triglycerides that are liquid at room temperature are called oils (tend to be unsaturated, and are derived from plants)
These are the lipids that store energy in our body; can be broken down into carbohydrates & released into the bloodstream to provide our cells with energy during periods of fasting
Structurally similar to triglycerides, but one of the fatty acid tails has been replaced by a phosphate group
An important component of cell membranes due to their amphipathic nature (possess both hydrophilic & hydrophobic ends)
Unique group of lipids in that they are based on a carbon ring structure rather than a fatty acid chain; are produced in liver
Like phospholipids, cholesterol is also amphipathic
Help to maintain cell membrane fluidity and produces hormones such as testosterone and estrogen
“Bad cholesterol” (low density lipoprotein or LDL) leads to plaque buildup in arteries called atherosclerosis
“Good cholesterol” (high density lipoprotein or HDL) carries low-density cholesterol back to liver to be broken down
LDLs can contribute to the build-up of plaque in arteries

This plaque can not only cause the obstruction of blood flow, but it can also cause blood clots that can travel to smaller arteries and cause blockages leading to strokes and heart attacks (more on this in Ch. 8)
Trans fats are a type of chemically altered unsaturated fatty acid high in LDL (“bad”) cholesterol (formed through hydrogenation)
Studies have linked the presence of trans fats in food products to heart disease
The addition of trans fats to food products has actually been banned many places, including New York City
Significantly fewer heart attacks and strokes have been reported since the implementation of these regulations… Canada recently followed suit
What are proteins, and why do we need them?
Like carbs & lipids, proteins are also composed of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. However, proteins also contain nitrogen, and atoms are arranged into molecules called “amino acids”.
Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins; many amino acids link together to form a polypeptide, and many polypeptides link together to form a protein.

Proteins do NOT provide energy for our cells. They play many other important roles in our bodies, including forming the structural components of cells, repairing damage to cells, speeding up chemical reactions (enzymes), and helping defend against disease (antibodies).

There are just 20 amino acids which comprise all proteins; 8 of these must be obtained through eating (our body is able to synthesize the rest). Proteins are found in meat, eggs, dairy products, and even some plants (e.g. legumes).
Enzyme found in nasal fluid and tears; kills bacteria by breaking down their cell walls
Membrane protein used make connections between structures inside and outside the cell
Structural protein in tendons, ligaments, skin and blood vessel walls; provides high tensile strength
Transport protein that allows red blood cells to carry oxygen throughout the body
Enzymes act by DECREASING the activation energy of reactants. The ability of an enzyme to facilitate a chemical reaction is influenced by a number of different factors:
An increase in temperature means an increase in the amount of energy within a chemical system; thus, enzyme activity also increases at higher temps
Beyond 37℃, however, proteins start to denature (break apart), so enzyme activity decreases
When proteins denature, they typically form a precipitate (for example, the skin that forms on milk when heated)
Most enzymes function optimally at a specific pH. When pH levels deviate from this range, the enzyme may begin to denature (unfold or break apart)
An enzyme can only catalyze a reaction if the appropriate substrate (the substance on which an enzyme acts) binds to its active site (receptor)
So, if substrate concentration increases, enzyme activity also increases (note that this is limited by the amount of enzyme present)

Identify the principal structures of the digestive system (mouth, esophagus, stomach, sphincters, small and large intestines, liver, pancreas, gallbladder)
Describe the processing of matter through the digestive system into the circulatory system
Two main divisions of the digestive system exist:
Accessory Organs (those which aid in digestion by secreting enzymes, but do not actually handle food)
Digestive Tract/Alimentary Canal (those which actually move food through the body)
Mouth, pharynx (throat), esophagus, stomach, small & large intestine, rectum, anus
Food is broken into smaller pieces (no chemical bonds broken)
Food molecules are broken into simpler molecules (chemical bonds broken)
Enzymes, acids, bile, other digestive chemicals
Increase surface area for enzyme action
Produce absorbable molecules (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids)
Food enters the digestive tract through the mouth. Here, teeth begin to break down food physically and enzymes secreted by salivary glands begin to break down food chemically.
Partially-digested food is then pushed down the esophagus into the stomach using a process called peristalsis.
In the stomach, muscle contractions continue physical digestion, and enzymes & stomach acids continue chemical digestion. Some water & salts are absorbed into the bloodstream.

Food then enters the small intestine. Enzymes from the pancreas & liver are secreted into the small intestine to finish chemically digesting food. The digested nutrients are then absorbed into the bloodstream through specialized structures called villi and microvilli.

After it is processed by the small intestine, food is then passed into the large intestine. Here, any remaining water & salt is absorbed. Bacteria in the large intestine also help release vitamins from food.
Next, waste enters the rectum where it is held until it is excreted. What remains of the food we have eaten exits the body through the anus.
Movement of food through the digestive tract
Salivary glands in the mouth secrete saliva, which contains an enzyme known as salivary amylase which breaks down starch into disaccharides. This is an example of chemical digestion.
Physical digestion also occurs in the mouth, where teeth chew up food into smaller pieces.
As you chew, your tongue pushes the bolus  (ball of food)  to the back of your mouth for swallowing.
The bolus enters the esophagus, moving towards the stomach through wavelike contractions of the esophageal tissue known as peristalsis

Before the bolus enters the stomach from the esophagus,        it must pass through the esophageal sphincter. The esophageal sphincter usually remains tightly shut to prevent stomach acid from splashing up into the esophagus       (a.k.a. heartburn).
Food undergoes both physical and chemical digestion in the stomach as well (chemical by the stomach acid, physical by the churning process that takes place as its muscular layers contract)
Pepsin, a protein-digesting enzyme, starts breaking down protein present in your food
A thick mucus prevents the acid from digesting the stomach lining (weak spots due to stress can lead to ulcers)
Very few substances are actually absorbed from the chyme that forms when your gastric juices mix with the bolus. At this stage, the substances in the chyme are still being broken down.
the stomach does absorb a small amount of water and salts into your bloodstream

it also absorbs alcohol and aspirin (This is why alcohol tends to reach your bloodstream relatively quickly. It also explains why, if you drink too much alcohol or take too much aspirin, it can lead to an upset stomach)
The pancreas delivers a fluid containing multiple enzymes to the small intestine, including...
The pancreas also secretes bicarbonate ions in order to raise the pH of materials entering the small intestine from the stomach.
The liver’s role in digestion is to secrete bile salts, which play a crucial role in the digestion of fats.

Bile salts help the lipases secreted by the pancreas break down fats in the small intestine by emulsifying lipids  (they make the fats more accessible by lipase). Emulsification is a physical process still, as no chemical reactions occur. The fats are simply broken into smaller pieces.
Hepatitis is an infection which targets the liver, resulting in cirrhosis (formation of scar tissue on the liver). Symptoms include weakness, exhaustion, and nausea.
Cirrhosis of the liver can also result from excess alcohol intake, as the helps filter toxins from your blood.
After bile is produced in the liver, it is sent to the gallbladder for storage in between meals. The gall bladder then “injects” bile salts as needed into the small intestine.
High cholesterol from excess fatty foods can cause gallstones to form; can be painful, and must be surgically removed.
Digesting and Absorbing Nutrients: The Small Intestine

Although some physical digestion occurs in the small intestine, its main function is to complete the chemical digestion of macromolecules  (carbs, proteins & lipids) and to absorb the resulting nutrients.
Receives enzymes from the pancreas to digest lipids, proteins, and starches.
Secretes additional enzymes to complete the digestion of these nutrients (e.g. enzymes such as lactase which break down disaccharides into monosaccharides).

The small intestine increases its ability to absorb nutrients by increasing its surface area. This is accomplished through segmentation (small folds), finger-like projections called villi, and even smaller projections called microvilli.
The small intestine works in conjunction with a number of accessory organs to finish digesting and absorbing different nutrients.
Once nutrients are fully digested/broken down into monomers, they can be absorbed into the bloodstream…
Glucose (monomer or carbs) and amino acids (monomers of proteins) are absorbed directly into the capillaries (small blood vessels) of the intestinal villi through active transport
Glycerol and fatty acids (monomers of lipids) are absorbed into the lacteals (lymph vessels part of the lymphatic system) of the intestinal villi through diffusion
The material that remains in the small intestine after nutrients are absorbed then enters the final part of the digestive tract: the large intestine.
The large intestine is only 1.5 meters long, but it has a greater diameter than the small intestine
Digestion does not actually occur in the large intestine. Its main function is to concentrate and eliminate waste materials through the rectum & anus
Additional salt & water is absorbed from chyme to form feces.
Bacteria play a vital role in breaking down any undigested food. These bacteria produce vitamins B-12 and K.
The Appendix: Not so useless after all…

It was previously believed that the appendix was a vestigial organ (has no purpose). However, it has recently been hypothesized that the appendix serves as a storage site for the “good” bacteria which aid in digestion.
As food is passed from the small intestine into the large intestine, the appendix is thought to add bacteria which aid in digestion as needed.
The appendix can become inflamed or infected if it absorbs  “bad” bacteria or toxins. Severe cases require surgical removal; failing to do so could result in death.
Symptoms of appendicitis include pain & tenderness in the lower right abdomen, nausea, vomiting, and fever.
Physical: chewing; Chemical: salivary amylase breaks down starch
Physical: churning; Chemical: pepsin breaks proteins, HCl aids digestion

A waste product of these processes is carbon dioxide; this is why we must exhale, to get rid of waste
Why do we need to breathe?
The two main functions of the
a) oxygen is brought to each cell in the body
b) carbon dioxide is removed from the body
notes: Every organisms needs to exchange materials with its environment. Unicellular organisms can make this exchange directly, but multicellular organisms (such as humans and animals) cannot make this exchange directly and rely on internal transport and exchange systems.
Oxygen is needed for cellular respiration to make ATP (not only to move muscles but ATP powers many other functions in the body) and CO2 is a waste of cell. resp. and needs to be removed.

Most CO₂ (≈70%) is carried as bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻) in plasma (after reacting with water in red blood cells).
A small amount (≈5–10%) is dissolved directly in plasma.
CO₂ travels mainly as bicarbonate ions.

this is why when young people are going through puberty their voice will deepen, especially for boys as their larynx grows bigger (bigger vocal chords). This is why their voice often cracks too as their bodies are getting adjusted to their new vocal cords.

Why are there cilia in our lungs?
Cilia are hair like projections that sweep mucus and dirt out of the lungs back up into the nose and throat to be coughed or sneezed out.

The site of gas exchange (carbon dioxide dissolved in the blood is exchanged for oxygen)

Divided into lobes- the right lung has three lobes, whereas the left lung has only two in order to make room for the heart

Ribs - protects the lungs and assists in breathing by enlarging the size of the thoracic cavity

1. External respiration is the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the air and the blood.
2. Internal respiration is the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the body’s tissue cells and the blood.
3. Cellular respiration is the series of energy-releasing chemical reactions that take place inside the cells. Cellular respiration is the final stage in respiration.
maintains homeostasis and provides energy for all cellular processes
notes: These stages basically track the path of oxygen from the environment to our cells and how it’s used to produce energy.
you know about cell resp a little bit, this is the same aerobic respiration we talked about last chapter

paragraphs: Inspiration (breathing in, inhaling) moves air from the external environment to the lungs inside the body
Expiration (breathing out, exhaling) moves air from the lungs back to the external environment
Two requirements of respiration are that:
the respiratory surface area must be sufficiently large for the O2/CO2 exchange to occur fast enough to meet the body’s need
respiration must take place in a moist environment so that the O2 and CO2 are dissolved in water
notes: delivering oxygen doesn’t just depend on the circulatory system but also on the lungs, → how much functional surface area is in the lungs
oxygen and co2 can only cross cell membranes when they are dissolved in water

paragraphs: Gas exchange occurs via diffusion between air in the alveoli and gases dissolved in the blood flowing through the adjacent capillaries.
The blood has a high concentration of CO2, so CO2 diffuses into the alveoli and is exhaled.
The alveoli have a high concentration of O2 after inhaling, so O2 diffuses into the blood, where it is then transported throughout the body so that cells can use it for cell respiration.
Oxygen enters the body when you inhale, makes its way into the alveoli of the lungs.
Oxygen then diffuses down its concentration gradient (from high to low concentration) from inside the alveoli into the capillaries/blood stream. The blood is now oxygenated.
CO2 from the capillaries diffuses down its concentration gradient (from high to low concentration) into the alveoli.
CO2 is then released from the body when we exhale.

Take a deep breath… What do you notice?
Breathing relies on the movement of gases from an area of high pressure to an area of low pressure via the action of the diaphragm…
the intercostal muscles contract and the rib cage expands

This increases the volume of the thoracic cavity and thus reduces air pressure within.  In order to equalize the external and internal air pressures, air moves into the lungs causing them to expand. The expansion is limited to the equalizing pressure and the elastic limit of the lung tissue.
Expiration (exhalation) is the reverse of inspiration.

2. Chest volume increases and air inside the thoracic
cavity is under less pressure than external air

diaphragm relaxes → diaphragm moves up into
2. Volume of thoracic cavity decreases causing air pressure in the lungs to increase
When exhaling, air moves from an area of high pressure (the lungs) to an area of low pressure (the external air)

Try holding your breath for a moment. Shortly you will feel an urge to resume breathing. This is not because you’re running low on oxygen, but is instead primarily triggered by a buildup of carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide is acidic in solution and will lower blood pH, which is the trigger for breathing.
Let’s look at how this works.
Cells make CO₂ when they use oxygen.
More CO₂ in the blood → pH drops (becomes more acidic).
Chemoreceptors in the brain detect this:
These sensors send signals to the medulla (brainstem), which controls breathing.
The medulla tells the diaphragm and intercostal muscles to work harder/faster.
Extra CO₂ is exhaled, and oxygen intake rises.
Blood pH and gas levels return to normal → the signal reduces (negative feedback).
Respiratory volumes can be measured with a device known as a spirometer…
Spirometers produce a spirograph which is a visual graph that measures how well and quickly you can move air into and out of your lungs.
Tidal volume = the volume of air that is inhaled and exhaled when breathing normally (at rest)
Inspiratory reserve volume = additional volume of air that can be taken into the lungs beyond regular (tidal) inhalation
Expiratory reserve volume = additional volume of air that can be forced out of the lungs beyond regular (tidal) exhalation
Vital capacity = total lung volume capacity (tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume + expiratory reserve volume)
Residual volume = the amount of gas that remains in the lungs after full exhalation

Flow of Blood Through the Body
Body/brain receives oxygenated blood from heart. Performs cell respiration & releases CO2 into bloodstream.
Newly deoxygenated blood from the body/brain returns to the heart.
Heart pumps the deoxygenated blood to the lungs, where CO2 is exchanged for O2
Newly oxygenated returns to the heart, which pumps it out to the body/brain.
Three main pathways of the circulatory system:
What supplies the muscle tissue of the heart itself with oxygen?

Oxygen and nutrients are delivered to the heart through capillaries embedded directly in the heart wall. These capillaries are supplied by two small arteries that branch off of the aorta. Deoxygenated blood is carried away in coronary veins.
Composed of 4 chambers: two atria (top chambers) and two ventricles (bottom chambers)
Right atrium and ventricle handle deoxygenated blood
Left atrium and ventricle handle oxygenated blood
..that the right heart is illustrated on the left side of a diagram, and the left heart on the right side of the diagram. This is because pictures will often show the heart from the front.
(aortic between left ventricle and aorta, and pulmonary between right ventricle and pulmonary artery)
The left & right sides of the heart are separated by a wall of tissue known as the septum.
The septum prevents oxygenated blood from mixing with deoxygenated blood.
Note that the muscle surrounding the left ventricle is much thicker than the muscle that surrounds the right ventricle.
This is because the left ventricle is responsible for pumping blood out to the entire body, while the right ventricle only needs to pump blood out to the lungs.
Valves ensure that blood flows only in one direction, and there is no backflow into a previous chamber
The ‘lub dub’ sound you hear when you hear your heart beat is from the valves shutting:
What if you had a leaky valve?

A leaky, or improperly sealing valve in the heart would allow the backflow and improper mixing of blood, and would also prevent the heart from being able to generate enough pressure during a contraction to pump blood
This could lead to reduced efficiency of circulation, and overexertion of the heart leading to enlargement and even heart failure

E.g. in the example to the right, the mitral valve is damaged. The mitral valve should be sealed when the left ventricle contracts, to ensure that all of the blood is being pushed out into the aorta. If the mitral valve is damaged, blood will flow back into the left atrium, instead of the aorta. The ventricle also has to pump even harder to get at least some of the blood to the aorta, which leads to the thickening of the ventricular muscles.
The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood (from the right ventricle to the lungs)
The pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood (from the lungs to the left atrium)
Often, arteries are thought of as blood vessels that carry oxygenated blood, while veins carry deoxygenated blood. However, this is not always the case…
Remember, the better way to define an artery is any blood vessel that carries blood AWAY from the heart. Conversely, veins are best defined as any blood vessel that carries blood TOWARDS the heart.
Once depleted of oxygen, blood returns to the right atrium of the heart through the superior and inferior vena cava
Blood moves through the right atrium to the right ventricle, where it is then pumped out of the heart via pulmonary arteries to the lungs. Here, CO2 will be exchanged for O2.
Oxygenated blood travels back to the heart where it enters the left atrium through pulmonary veins.
Blood flows into the left ventricle and is pumped out of the heart via the aorta, where it then travels to other areas of the body.

If you have a smart watch, it may be able to perform an ECG and look for signs of atrial fibrillation (AFib). AFib  is an irregular, often rapid heartbeat caused by disorganized electrical signals in the atria. This makes the upper chambers quiver instead of contracting properly, leading to poor blood flow and an increased risk of clots, stroke, and heart failure.

Note, that a smart watch is not the most accurate tool for these, as it only uses one lead, as opposed to a regular ECG which uses 12 leads. If you ever have any concerns about your heart, always see your doctor!!
Blood pressure is the pressure exerted against the walls of the arteries as blood is transported throughout the body
Measured as a ratio of systolic/diastolic pressure (120/80 is normal)
Maximum pressure during ventricular contraction = systolic pressure
Minimum pressure when ventricles are relaxed = diastolic pressure
Cardiac output is the amount of blood pumped by the heart per unit of time
Used to indicate extent of oxygen delivery to tissues

Blood coming to the skin from the body’s interior is usually warmer than the skin itself. Through the process of diffusion, heat is lost from the body as more blood passes by the skin. The greater the heat gradient, the faster heat is lost through the body surface.
The nervous system can control the loss of heat by the body by adjusting the amount of blood that flows closer to the skin’s surface.
The process of blood vessels expanding and moving towards the skin to release heat is referred to as vasodilation
The process of blood vessels contracting and moving away from the skin to conserve heat is referred to as vasoconstriction

divide into two different types of B-cells: Memory B-cells and Plasma cells:

Memory B-cells display antibodies (proteins) that match the antigens (proteins) presented by that particular pathogen. They remain in the bloodstream so that if they ever encounter that pathogen again, they can quickly call a phagocyte to the scene.

Plasma cells produce antibodies that recognize and attach to the antigens of specific pathogens, essentially slowing the pathogen down and marking it for destruction by phagocytes. Antibodies remain in the bloodstream so that next time the pathogen enters the bloodstream, phagocytes can quickly destroy it.
Every vaccine is different. However, they are all based on the principle of providing people with antibodies against specific antigens.

Most vaccines involve injecting a “deactivated” version of a pathogen into your body. This means that the pathogen cannot reproduce and infect your tissues, but it does contain the antigen markers on it’s cell surface.

When your body detects the presence of the deactivated pathogen, it still launches a full-scale immune response, even though there is no actual threat. This is why people often develop a fever or feel “sick” after receiving a vaccine.
Once your body detects the pathogen, Helper T-cells recruit B-cells, which differentiate and start producing antibodies against that pathogen’s antigens.
Once you have those antibodies, you will be able to fight off the “real pathogen” more easily should it ever try to infect your cells. This is what gives you “immunity” against that pathogen.

Many vaccines require a booster shot after a few years, as these antibodies (which are just proteins) tend to break down over time. This is also why elderly people tend to have a weaker immune system compared to younger individuals.

In humans, blood type can be classified in two different ways: according to the ABO and Rhesus blood groups. These groups are differentiated according to the antigen markers found on the membrane of each red blood cell…
Rh (-) individuals do not display Rhesus antigens
Blood Type A individuals display A-antigens and produce antibodies against B-antigens. So, Type A individuals can only receive blood from other Type A individuals (or Type O).
Blood Type B individuals display B-antigens and produce antibodies against A-antigens. So, Type B individuals can only receive blood from other Type B individuals (or Type O).
Blood Type AB individuals display both A and B antigens, and do not produce antibodies against either antigen. So, Type AB individuals can receive blood from either Type A, Type B, Type AB, or Type O

Blood Type O individuals display no antigens, and produce antibodies against both A and B-antigens. So, Type O individuals can receive blood only from other Type O individuals (however, their blood is accepted by all types)

Not only do our red blood cells present various antigens depending on our DNA; antibodies against other blood types are produced by our white blood cells. This makes you unique blood type incompatible with any other blood type (with some exceptions of course…)
Cells that show “clumping together” or agglutination indicate rejection by blood cells.
AB+ individuals have all three types of antigen on their red blood cells, and therefore do not produce any antibodies. As a result, they can receive blood from any donor (“universal recipient”)
O- individuals have no antigens present on their red blood cells, so they can donate to individuals of all blood types (“universal donor”)
Erythroblastosis fetalis can occur with subsequent pregnancies if the mother is Rh- but her first child was Rh+
